Mr. Logh went on to say that he" looked upon Irish landlords with a feeling akin to pity. They I were situated between the devil and the deep sea, I and when they were not openly robbed by their tenants they wore more slowly, hut quite as sure- ly, fleeced by whatever Government happened to be in power." The member for the Newton Divi- sion neglected to explain which was " the devil " and which "the deep sea:: However, this much is beyond question ; he ought at once to resign his seat. If he is an honest man, he cannot go on 11 supporting is Government which slowly but surely fleeces Irish landlords.

div.head: SAILOR'S FREAK AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A SAILOR'S FREAK AT RUNCORN.

James Thompson, a sailor was brought before the Runcorn magistrates yesterday charged with being drunk and disonlerty and also with assault- ing James Burgess, a dock constable. About half-past two that morning P.C. Benlield found the prisoner making night hid.uo by singing and shouting in Percires Lane, and ordered i him away. The prisoner jumped upon the Lint vessel he came to in the dock and from the manner he acted Burgess was afraid he would fall into the dock and be drowned. The captain said be did not belong to the ship and com- plained of the disturbance he was causing. The prisoner, however, refused to leave, aud the two officers fastened a rope around his waist and haukd him about 15 feet up the side of the dock. Ile had 14 previously assaulted the dock constable. Ile was ordered to pay Li Ida. -Ht., or go to goal for • month.

div.head: TENANTS' LEAGUE FOR IRELAND.
div.p: A TENANTS' LEAGUE FOR IRELAND.

The Fmeman's Journal and United Ireland '' publish the following We are authorised by Mr. Parnell to : announce that a tenants' leave will be formed lintnedi. ately in Ireland to protect tenants against the combine- tioust landlords. This League will be the official act lof the whole Irish party, and will shortly In established at a convention. The " Freeman's Journal' says the I details were settlwl last swvk by Messrs. Parnell, Sexton, Otßrien, Davitt, and :Harrington. The constitution of the League will make It invulnerable to legal attack. If Mr. Balfour desires to stop it he must pass a new coercion act.
AI ! ACCIDENT ON THE CONTINENT. SIXTEEN LIVES LOST.

VIENNA, TrESDAT 7,lloll,—TelP2ratus from Bucharest announce another terrible railway accident, which hate penes' yestenlay through a pointsinan's mistake. A passenger train coming froin Bucharest ran into a goods train near the station of Ciulnita. Both engines were smashed to pieces, together with the tender, luggage van, and the ling passenger carriage. Fifteen passes- gets were killed, and many badly hurt. The stoker of the passenger train W:44 burnt to death. A train with medical aid has left for the seentl of the disaster.

div.p: SALE OF WORK AT WARRINGTON RECTORY.

A sale of work was opened on Wednesday after- noon in the Rectory Grounds, Warrington, by Mrs. George Dewhurst. of Oughtrington Park, Lymm, in aid of the Ladies Association for Foreign Missions , in the Archdeaconry of Warrington. Inn tot on the lawn three stalls were erectisl, two of them containing a large variety of useful and fancy , articles contributed by numerous ladies in the , district, and the other stall- containing a tine di.- tiny of Rowers. The stalls were attended to by the , I following ladies :—Miss hmailbent, Misses Rylands, ' I Misses Stubs, Miss Withington, Misses 'Nekton, l Misses (Neenah. Mi. Dun, Miss Harvey, Misses Litton, Miss E. White, Mrs. Woods, senr., Mrs. IV. Woods, Mrs. Fairelough, Mrs. Francomb, Mrs. Clayton, Mrs. Wileocks, Mrs. Langham, Misses Robinson. Dewhund, Mrs. Glazebrook Rylantls, and Mrs. Lyon,. of Appleton IND In a Becond tent refreshments • were dispensed during the afternoon and evening. By permission of the colonel and officers tho band r of the Liverpool Regiment was present from the . , barracks, and played several selections. Among ' those present at the opening of the sale of work were the Rector (the Rev. F. WI Willis), the Rev. F. hI. Reichardt (curate of Lyinin),, ! Lieutenant Clayton. Mr. J. D. 'Nekton, and Mr.: IVent Davies. Before Mrs. Dewhorst declared the , sale own, the Roctor explained that the pniceeds i would he divided between the Society for the Pro- I pagation if the Gospel and the Diocese of North China. Mr.. Dewhurst, in opening tire proceedings, said she had all her life taken a very great interest in [ht work of foreign missions, and it had been a great pleasure to her to accept the kind invitation, ; of Sir, and Mrs. Willis to open that sale of work , which she hoped would be very successful. div.head: THREE MEN KILLED AT PORTSMOUTH.
div.p: THREE MEN KILLED AT PORTSMOUTH.

An ambient happened at Partsmouth onWednesday by I which three men were killed. Abont two years ago the C,orwration erected tripod sheare on the lower quay capable of bearing a strain of 30 tons. On 'Wednesday the boilers of the old Enchantress yacht were being re- moved, and the largest having been deposited on the ground, was being refilled to it. removed to a more suit- able spot %Olen the strain of the 15-ton boiler ivated on one leg of the shears. The strocture was seen to vibrate while the chain encircling the boiler snapped. There were twenty men working at the cajotanaand as soon as they saw the shears tottering they ran in all direc- tions. Three of them, tom.' respectively Tubbs, Williams, and Hubbard, ran right mmna the falling structure. Tubbs was immediately knocked down and erushol to death, Williams had his brains knocked out and Hubbard received such injurim that he died shortly afterwards. Several other emu were injured.

div.head: ASSAULT BY A WIDNES WORKS MANAGER.
div.p: ASSAULT BY A WIDNES WORKS MANAGER.

Samuel Vernon, of Peol.st., stated to be a manager at the Widnes Alkali Works, was brought before ' Mr. Brundrit and Dr. Steele to answer a charge of , having unlawfully...gel and beaten Jane limd- burn, the landlady of the Albion Inn, Peel-st. --Mr.; &Wynne Humphreys appeared forth° complainant, and Mr. J. Si'. Knowles, of Widnes, defended.—lt was alleged that on Sunday night, about half-past ten, Mrs. Bradburn, her servant, and a master labourer named Pierce II uglies, of Weston,were just . arriving home alter having spent the afternoon at I Halo. As they passed the defendant he said "You are fairly in it. and when asked what he : meant, he replied to the son f know more attest your mother than this man (Hughes) dues." ;lie followed up his words by knocking the son down by a blow .nt the mouth, and upon the eoinplitinant remon- strating Inc treated her in a similar manner. Holore Hughes could interfere Inc won also knockml down in the gutter. Upon Mrs. Itradlnern rising to her fivt, the defendant again knctiked her down and struek her on I the knee and breast, eausingher a black eye. Afterwards 1 he again felled Hughes to the ground, and upon a man I named William Daniels appearing on the scene the defendant ran hoine.—ln erowrexamination Mrs. Brad- burn said she was living atiwt fniin her husband. . . . . .

kept a " free anl eas-y at her public-hou.si. She was only in one public-house during the Sunday afternoon and had one bitter beer. When she met the defendant, she was walking arm in arm with Hughes and with the nerved—fly Mr. Ilinnplireys ; Her hus- band had been ill for 11 or 12 years and was in a lunatic .sylum.-1111g1USS on crosswicatnination stated that Mrs. Bradburn had one bitter beer and several swill whiskies. —For the defence Mr. Knowles statedthat oath, defend- ant paxsel the coinplainant and her friends, Hughes gave a lurch and sent hint off the footpath. Ile said "you might be fair and decent," whereupon they changed their course, and followed hint. Hughes threat- ened to black his eyes for him and struck him, and he , returned the blow. The complainant then gave him a smack on the fare, and he pushed her away. The son ! came tip and he gave him a blow, and then ran to his house as fast as he could. Afterwards several of the complainant's friends attempted to break the door of his house in. Mr. Knowles informed the Bench that Mrs. Bradhum had been charged with keeping her house , open after hours, and she suspected the defendant of having informed the ponec. This was a conspiracy to disgrace the defendant and rain his character. j Dr. McDougall said he had known the defendant for 20 years. He had acquired property by his own industry ; and was a most exemplary man. If he had been guilty jof an asiatilt, it must hare been under the greatest j provocation.—Tbe magistrates considered the assault I proved, and imposed a tine iif 20s and costs.

div.head: POISONING MYSTERY IN DERBYSHIRE.
div.p: THE POISONING MYSTERY IN DERBYSHIRE.

At the Alfreton Police Court lleorge Horton, a miner. I has been committed for trial for the wilful murder of his daughter Kate, aged eight years. It is alleged against the prisoner that the deceased suffered from thirst, and asked for a drink of water. Her father in answer to her nattiest, gave her some blue-looking liquid. In an flour after taking it, she died, and an examination of the body showed that death was due to strychnine poisoning. It WAS stated in evidenee that Kisoner had threatened to poison another daughter, who had left home through I ill-treatment.

div.p: BURNLEY GAZ ZTTE, February 23rd.
raHE lot of those who toil from day to day in the bowels of the ‘2" earth is not a very agreeable one. Apart from the terrible _ _ _ . .

risks of which we are so often reminded by a calamitous explosion, with all its thrilling scenes, the collier has to pursue his work at times under circumstances of great hardship. Mr. Moses Knowles, of 109, Oxford Road, Burnley-, has had some experience of the trying conditions of labour in sonic of the deeper coal mines of this country. He relates how he has repeatedly had to work for hours crouched in ten or twelve inches of water and the cold liquid at the same time dropping all over his body from above. Happily such conditions of employment are almost unknown in the Burnley district, but Mr. Knowles has had to ?mounter them in other mining surf:Ter in consequence. He first I 1 commenced with pains in his head, which gradually extended I to other parts of the lxxly.* " I got so low," said Mr. Knowles, "that I was obliged to be covered

with blankets and have a chair i close to the fire even on a warm day. It was only then that I could feel anything like warmth. My legs got so weak that I. had to have the help of a stick to get across the floor. I was terribly troubled with indigos- tom. nervous debility, and disease of the liver and kidneys, and had constant attacks of cramp in di.. stomach. For many weeks I suffered dreadfully, writhing in agony for hours together, and got so weak that it was painful to speak, let alone trying to move. Medicine only Sl4. RENTs, Sir,-1 see that the member tor the Newton Division haa lasn talking about the way in which landlords are robbed in Ireland. It. mak, it ind that they are always being robbed either by the tenants or by the partkadar Government which happins to be in power. If hethinks, sir, that the present Government is a Government of robbers I wonder how it is that he is always so ready to support them through thick and thin. Surely he cannot do this unlem he wblies it to he understand that he is perfectly willing to be in allianee with a band of rob- ber, It seems to me that the beat thing he siuld 10 wonld be to throw up the sponge and have nothing to with a dishonist body of men.

_ I cannot help asking, if ho Wilts upon it as robbery that Irish landlords should have their rents reduced to a fair figure, what he thinks of the conduct of his father who takes out of Warrington to muck money in the way of groom] rents without contributing anything to the rates of the borough. Is that robbery .? The people who live in Warrington, tradesmen and others, are called upon to may rates because they are understood to benefit by the work of the emporation in giving value to property and security to pros pos v. Where would be the value of and when. would he ihe security to property if it were not for the well-paved and well-lighted streets and roads, and a bade of policemen to look after everybody's property? Anal, without these things, where woula be the value of the land on which Mr. ',nil makes his rent charges? I have an idea mvself, that the real robbers of this country are the landlords, who Nom, everything they can out of the people in the shape of ground rents and royalties, and don't give a penny hack in the shop., of rates and, If Ido not make a mistake, there will he such an ;agita- tion on this question before long as will Guise some of these grabbers to surnsider a portion of their ill-gotten gains. Instead of backing op a Government of plun- derers, such as is the pnasent Government, acconliog to Mr. T. W. lamb, lie would do well to back out of all con- nection with them and, by devoting his time and eniT- gies to this subject, help honest men to get their own.— Yours, Lac., . _„ ........ div.head: MR. WILLIAM IMOGLE'S LATEST WRIGGLE . . . . '
div.p: MR. WILLIAM IMOGLE'S LATEST WRIGGLE . . . . '

Pie-In Mr. niggles letter of the 22nd June he made a distinct assertion to the effect that the delivery pipes from the depots to Longford would silt up, and that as a fat's little while ago an obstruction did take place, and in theexamination of &certain bend lathe pipes it was found so stopped up [bat s man could only get his three fingers therein." In my reply of the nth nit., I said that thisstatement id Mr. Diggle's wasan absolute fabrication from beginning to end. I now repeat that assertion emphatically, and further, if Mr.Diggle will not submit to public examination the authority upon which he makes such serious charges, then I say his conduct can only be explained by one of two reasons—either he has no authority and has invent.' thestatements himself, or else he has found his source of information to be of so questionable a character that he dare not expose it. Again, Mr. Diggle refers to what he calls the " burst " in Oliver-nt. on June 17th last, and says that "either Mr. Henry Itatsirts does not know of this, or he lies." Well, sir, I knew oil about it when I wade mine of the 27t1s ult., and I did not lie. I now repeat the statement which then used and again say "that since they were first laid until now, the pipes have never been uncovered for any purpose whatsoever eottnected with the object for which they were intended." Now, sir, what are the facts spun which Diggle has constructed his ridiculous charge. On Whit Friday, the raving and Sewerage men were instructed to open out the ground for the alteration of a sewer in Oliver-nt. They, not knowing the position of thedelivery pipes which en,s thiS street, accidentally hit one of the pipes with a pick which caused a small hole in the pipe about the size of a pta through which the liquor 0 squirted." The accident was immediately reported and (Imply. made good. Thin is Ow only ocrwonn on which the pipes have been uncovered, 21111, 2a your f. readers will at once see, it was for "no purpose whets,- ewer connected with the object for which they were intended.- To persons who have any knowledge upon the subject, the fact that the liquor " squirted" with auch force through no small a hole, affords positive proof that on" ritting 'can be going on. Lastly, ?dr. Diggle says "if the pipes are as clear now an at the first, why the severe extra pressure to get the stuff through." This, sir, is another gratuitous fib of Mr. DigglcS. No severe extra pressure is necuissary, and consequently none is applied. The rest of Mr. Diggle's letter is an personal that I shall not notice it further than to any, that it is written in such bad taste and sin utterly unlike my old friend, that I feel bound to attribute its authorship tan much smaller individual than he whs. name it bears.—Yours truly, July 10th, 1989.

Tho new bride's at Wildegrove, o we hove before r•splatued takes theplace of a foot road which go. , through the fiellk from Thelwall, and a diversion of the ' river hare being necessary for the prosecution of the Canal works the road woo necessarily cut through, and this bridge has been erected to replace that part of the road taken away. The river diversien is now completed and the water diverted into it. It is 600 yards long, and the bottom width 100 feet, with an average depth of 20 feet. The banks are 'doped 11 to 1, and are pitched with stones of a thickness of 1 foot 9 incl.. The bridge is situated at the eastend of this eutting,and !is of the stiffened auspension type. It is a light and ele- gant structure. Its length from endto end is 214 fee Land ! the span between the pillars 106 feet. The piers consist of east iron cylinders lin. thick, 6 feet diameter, and 6 feet : deep. These have been bated together, and mink 15ft. , below the bottom of the river diversion. The height of the piers above the bottom of the river diversion is 31ft. ; , on these piers the towers an. bolted, and these consist of tour legsof channel iron rivet's] back to back, and the , piers are filled up solid with concrete. To the stddlen at • the top of the towers are attached the suspension or tie rods. which support the rolled iron insta on which the roadway is carried. The roadway consists of Memel deal Marring 21ins. thick, and , there is a handrailing nt each side of the bridge. Below the handrail, proteytion against falling through iatop- plied by wire fencing, which has a rack attachment at !each end for tightening up. Each end of the bridge is ' supported on walings, the waling being bolted to piles 1 which have been driven a considerable distance in the ground. AND TIM TEACHERS OF WA RRIN( ;TON

Sir Gilbert Greene'', the member for Warrington, terms to have succeeded in giving offence ton by no means insignincant portion of the constituency. Of late there has been a go. d deal of tliSelOglii/li ill regard to the Education Code, and the Warrington and District Teachers' Association, which is affiliated with the National Union of Teachers, naturally took the matter into consideration. Early in May, at It meeting of the local ASlOCilltioll, it was deemed desirable that a deputation should wait upon Sir Gilbert (Deena, a, the representative for Warrington, for the purpose of laying before him various suggestions for the alteration of the proposed new code. In due course a deputation was appointed, and the Secretary of the Association was authorised to write to `'lr Gilbert, asking him to name a, early a day ILS possible on which he would be willing to meet the deputation, owing to the nrgency of ;lie matter. The Secretory followed out his instruction,, and received a reply from Sir Gilbert on the ..17. th of May to the effect that he was out of town, but on his return he would arrange a day on wick to meet the deputation, either in Warrington or Walton. Subseqnently a aecond meeting of the ASSOCilitioll wao held, to arrange who should speak, and what representations dumb' be made to Sir Gilbert. No communication, has, however, been received (nun Sir Gilbert, and. as the time 'luring wiich action might be reken with regard to the onle has now passed, the members of the Assomr.tion naturally feel somewhat aggrieved at their proposal for an interview not having been carried out. It does seem as though a slight had been put upon the Areoeiat ion, which, it. should be noted, is in no sense apolitical organis- ation ; but, perhaps, after all it is not thy will but the memory of the member for Warrington that is at fault. When a man iS SO deeply immured in parliamentary woak as Sirelilbert is so well known to be, it ion very simple matter for a trifle like the request of a portion of IRs constituency to be over- looked. Sir Gilbert is,usually,so urbane and so very bland, that it is almost impossible to conceive that the slight was intentional. At any rate, it is more charitable to put it down to forgetfulness, and it may not he out of place to suggest that Sir Gilbert would be better able to cope with his artluousduties by the aid of a" Privete Secretary." or, if he is too poor to engage one, he might resign his twat and give himself a holiday for the rest of his life. • ALLEGED SHOCKING OUTRAGE BY SHIP CANAL WORKMEN.
THE VICAR OF TOP:WALL GOES TO THE RESCUE.

On Monday night a widow named Mary Rooney I living at Newfield, Lymmovas indecently assaulted, on the highway to Lyium, opposite Thelwall Vicar- age, by a number of men. While the vicar of Mel- wall, the Roe. T. I'. Williamson, was sitting in his house about half-past ten o'clock, he heard a noise an if someone was choking end struggling on the road which runs close by. Ile and his son, Mr 0. R. Williamson, at once went out, and, although very dark at this spot, which is covered by trees, they saw a stool, group of persona near the hedge. some of them on the ground. Some men got up and ran away, but Mr. G. R. Williamson ran after and got bold of one of them, whom he handed over to his father, and then went after another who, however, turned round and knocke,l him down. The man whom he had previously caught also made his escape. On coming hack they found Mrs. Rooney standing on the roadway and a man named Priestley. P.C. Millington. of Orappen- hall. vms at once sent for and quickly arrived at the spot. Rooney complained that she had been outraged by two of the men, while others held her. She also accused Priestley, who had remained on the spot, of being one of her assailants. Rooney was taken by P.C. Millington to the police Aker at Thelwall, and the latter escorted her to Isymm. Subsequently, John Prieatley, engine driver, Frank Cox and Henry Jenkins, navvies, were arrested on a charge of having been concerned in the outrage. All these men live at the Thelwall butt, and are employed on the Ship Canal. It is understood that a fonrth man is being sought after by thepolice.

div.head: COMING QUESTION IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: A COMING QUESTION IN WARRINGTON.
A NEW BRIDGE WANTED.
WHER.E lIAS IT TO BE?

it often strikes roe that we in Warrington will. , before very long, be face to face with a question which will even eclipse that of the intercepting depots and their reputed smells. The quentton : allude to is that of improving the means of com- munication between the two parts of the borough ' which lie on different sides of the river. At present, as we all know, the solo connecting link, the only , roadway for general traffic, is a bridge, 'solid and substantial, but not very wide. As far as it goes! the present britlge is no doubt all that could be : , desired, but t here are abundant judicial°. that , before long it will fall far short of the rmoirements r of the case. Let a person stand upon the bridge , almost any day in the week, and especially on , Saturdays and Wedtiemlays, anti lie will be • quickly forced to the comilusion that very fre- • qnently the traffic is already fully as heavy as it can conveniently accommodate. Yet tini. traffic t is at present constantly increasing, and there is to ; prospect. still more rapid increase. The present ! increase is due to the growth of Latchford, jest now the most progressive part of the borough, and the , Ship Canal undertaking gives plenty of reasons for anticipating a great future increase. The position then is this -a bridge barely sufficient for the traffic , of to-day, but, almost certainly, totally inadequate , for the traffic of the future. I can imagine some , hour-faire individual-- one of the let-things-alone- until-you-can-let-them-alone-no-longer persouage , say" What of that? Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." But surely that is not the best , attitude our local leaders can take up. As soon as it becomes evident tbat a problem ' must be faced before long, the sooner it is faced , : the better, and tins applies with special force ' lathe providing of commodious roadways. How many difficulties with regard to street widenings , and improvements would hare been avoided if town turd municipal authorities had been more in the habit of looking a few years ahead? To me it seems almost certain that the local authorities will, in the course of a very few years, be compelled to take into consideration some scheme for improving the communication between the two parts of the borough, and this being so you will perhaps allow me a little awe to ventilate a few ideas on the subject. Assuming that the additional accommo- dation will be provided by a new bridge rather than widening the existing structure, the question at once arises. where will be the most convenient and useful site for • second bridge? lisa the south the traffic passes along two main arteries, Wildermool- road, and Knutsford-road, but it is only reason- able and prudent to anticipate that there will within a few years be an immense accession to and from the Ship Canal Company's docks. It is also to bo remembered that a rimy road is projected, tO con- nect Wilderspool-rd. with Knutsford-rd. somewhere near St. Mary's-st. and a little higher up than Mr. Edelsten's works. This new roal seems to have been planned with a view to relieving the pressure at tlm Wilderspool level crossing by diverting vehicles from Wilderspool-road to linutsford-road on the one hand and from Knutefool-road to Wilderspool-road on the other, but it will fail en- tirely to relieve the congested traffic at the bridge, which will probably need relief fully as much as , that at the level crossing. Taking all these circum- stances into account, does it not appear that what is wanted in the future is to continue this new road across Knutsford-road, through Victoria-terrace, some of the houses of which would,of course, have to come down, and over the river by a bridge into Howley meadows at a point a short distance lower ' down than Mersey Mills, the roadway to be then continued across the meadows into, say, Napier-st. Consider for a moment how this would meet the necessities of the case. In the first place a very large portion of the growing traffic to and from the , higher parts of Latchford would at once be diverted , into the new thoroughfare, and the same may be said of the traffic to and from the Stockton Heath direction and the eastern parts of Warrington. A r Wilderspool dray, for instance, bound for the die- trict around Church-st., or for some place along , Manchester-rd., would, as a matter of preference, ' be turned off to the right from the Causeway along I the new road and across the new bridge, and , the same might he said with regard to a ,1 considerable proportion of the vehicular traffic I through Stockton Leath. To make the slew read vittoutof triiieersnooC Mintscows wit bout making a convenient passage over the river attire end of it, would be tittle better than throwing money away. for what driver coming from Stockton Wrath WOUIII make so wide a circuit when he knew that at the end of it he would still have to crush his way over a congested bridge. Another incidental but very important advantage of a Midge at or near the point I refer to would be the relief that it would afford to the already intolerable state of affairs at Market Gate on busy days. It was only two or three months ago that a member of the Town Council complained that when he was driving from Latchford to the Central Station he had to allow himself about ten minutes for prob able stoppages at Market Gate. With the new bridge all these ineonveniences would be swept away. A person driving a conveyance or vehicle of any kind from Latchford to the Central Station, to Winwick- et., the Market ground, or indeed any of the more northerly parts of Warrington, would but, need to cross over the new bridge and strike thmugh Napier-st., Academy-st., and Scotland-road, and in that way he would not only avoid the existing narrow bridge but also the almost chronic glut at , Market Gate. To a driver from Stockton Heath the advantage would be still greater, for be would avoid not only the old bridge and Market Gate, but , that great nuisance, the level crossing, as well. - It may be raised as an objection to this proviso] that the streets in Ilowley direction have been laid out without any suspicion that Rome of them might 1 in time become important thoroughfares, and that they are altogether too narrow and mean and circuitous for main streets. There is no doubt something in this argument, though it is hardly sufficient to condemn such a scheme of public improvement esthete referred to. The central fact, that before many years are past additional means of passing the river will have to be provided, still : remains, and to me there seems no better plan for making this provision than by placing a bridge at ' the point named above. If there are others who , can formulate a better method for meeting thel' difficulty, I Aall glad to hear of it.

SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT COLBORNE. Early nn Thmeelay morning John Wright wan. instantly killed whilst engaged in working at K Evans and Co.'s mines at Golborne, near Newton-le- Willows. The following extract is of e,pecial interest in view of the mischief that might be done by the Sugar Convention Bill 4. A great increr, in the price of sugar, says Mr. Wood gravely, would be fatal to us. So long a+ sugar is cheap, no matter bow large a crop of fruit we had we should be aide to take it. The price of jam depends almost entirely upon what we have to give for the sugar, and it has already risen from/16 to £2.1 per ton, so that we are uneasy upon the matter."

div.head: CLAIM FOR DAMAGES.
div.p: CLAIM FOR DAMAGES.
ACCIDENT AT THE "SUNLIGHT" SOAP WORKS.

On Thursday, at the Warrington County Court,. before lao Honour Judge t foulkes and a jury, an action was heanl in which William Brown, aged fourteeen, claimed. through his brother, John , Brown, 1:50 from Messrs. Lever Brothers, proprie- tors of the Sunlight Soapworks at Warrington, as damages for injuries sustained by him in come:- , queue" of the alleged negligence of the defendants. Mr. Bickford. Li verpoool (instructed by Messrs. : Jenkins and Bosworth. Warrington) appeared for ! the plaintiff, and Mr. Yates, Manchester (instructed ' by Messrs. Rowley (Page and Rowley), Manchestel, represented the defendants.

Mr. Piekford, in opening the case for the plaintiff, ' mid that the action was liniught under the Employers,' Liability A--the recover damages front the defendants for personal injuries occasioned throogh their alleged ' negligence. Ile explained hat the defendants inanufax- . tuns! them own boxes for packing the soap which they , made. Printinss machines were also in esse by them mr Iproviding the lettering outside the boxes, and it was while engaged at one of these machinis: that the toy , Brown cause by Isis asimdent oat the 6511 March last. On the thy hi qUeStioll he was putting a hard Isitween toe rollers, when his Cot slipped, in Oniseipence of the Boor not having hien properly cleaned, and, in endeavouring r..i..,gvhetrelayreivivas.d crattl:tt would ii, the iii • probability have to Ise amputates!. He (Mr. Ifickforth submitted that the defendants were guilty of negligence in not having caused the machine to be protected by a . guard, which would have pnwented such an accident, Messrs. Lever did, after Use accident, put up a guard. but it only nimained a few days in front of the In:Whines. Ha further contended that the defendants were guilty of another act of negligence in allowing the flair in front ' .if the Madan.eo to remain in a dirty and slippery state.. The injury sustained by the plaintiff wassail, that in • all probability his ann would have to be amputated. At any rate, he was permanently injured, and had alto- griller lost the use of his right arm. Ile contended that it was tlie duty of employers reasonably to sea that thu machinery to which they put people to work was iu as safe a condition as it practically could be. There was alni negligence in allowing the floor to be slippery.— William Brown, in his evidence, said he had been employed nearly ninetoin months by the defendants, and had worked at the sainting machine for the past two noinths. The accident to his arm happened on a Wednes- day, and the floor, which was smileed with soap and oils, had nut been cleaned since the previous Saturday. Ile had his right hand on the board in front of Use machine when his foot slipped, and in falling his hand and arm were drawn between the rollers.—Or. Bmith,the braise Aurgeoll at the Warrington Infirmary, stated that the boy hail been under treatment at that institutiothand was still an nut-patient. Ile consideresl it very probable that the boy's arm would have to be amputated.—Other evidence was given by men from the works of Messrs. Crosfield and Sons, to the effect that the machines were .1 unsafe and dangerous if used without a guard.

Mr Yates, for the defence, contended at length that the accident was not due to the negligence of the defend-! ants. He denied that it was owing to the machine being : unfenced. The floor was not slippery in the sense that • I had been described by tin witnesses for the plaintiff, : 'anti if there was any danger in the machine being work- ed without a guard, or in the floor being slippery, the ! boy would know this, but he had never made ' any complaint. If boys were careless at their w!,rk, and an accident occurred iu consequence, tile, employers were not responsible. The machines in question were perfectly sate if roasonable care ! were exercised in attending to them. Mr. Yates then called several witnesses for the defence, including Mr. Winter, the manager of the works, who said that in 116 opinion there was no danger attendant on the working ! of the machines. Two witnesses engaged in the menu- factoring 4d similar machinery gave evidence to the ! STRIP effect, and cm, of them said that he never yet saw . printing inatdiines fenced. There was no necessity for ! the machinm in question to be fenced. If ahoy was! reasonably careful, there was no chance of such an ! accident Lappeuing. The inachim, was like an ordinary mangle, only the rolkrs were wider apart.

Mr. Tates then quoted various legal decisions in tavour , of the defence, and, Mr. Oickfcial having replied, his ! Honour annulled up. The jury then retired, afterwards mturning into Court with a verdict for the plaintiff, , to whom they awarded £4tl 16s. Od. damages, with ! costa.

. . A New York correspondent telegraphs c—Sullivan, the , pugilist, was arrested on Thnrsday at Nashville, 'lnn- neon', when he arrived on his way north. The arnst I was made by order of the Governor of Missiwippi, the ! State in which the recent fight occurred. The police entered the railway carriage, anal seeing Sullivan encica- , voured to handcuff hitn. After a brief struggle Sullivan WAS taken front the carriage and hustled in a cab. In the scuffle he drew back to knock down a policeman, when the chief of the police fold. pistol to his face and told him that if he struck the man he would kill him. Thr officers now took Johnson, Sullivan's backer, who resisted vigorously, but finally began to ere with pain. Mike Cleary, Sullivan's other backer, hid d g the excitement, and one other named Lynch jumped off the train. Only Johnson and Sullivan were I detained, though the others were wanted. It is a quis-, tion whether the police did not exceed their authority in I arresting Sullivan in one State on the order of the , 6oventor of another State, and it may be impossible to hold him but the Governor of Mississippi baa offered a reward of 1,000 dollars for Sullivan's arrest, and if he escapes this titne it is ahnost certain that he will be , rearrested. Kilrain is on his way north, tnaking every effort to avoid arrest. Public opinion is with the ' Government, and it is hoped that it will succeed in put- , ling Sullivan in prison.
